characters: Zaara: an eight-year-old Ghanaian girl in a blue-and-yellow school uniform and tidy white headscarf, holding a blue colouring marker.
Akrofi: her nine-year-old classmate in a matching yellow uniform shirt and blue shorts, holding a green colouring marker.
Madam Salamatu: their kind class teacher in an emerald-and-gold African-print dress.

narrationPlan.voice: Lively at the start; calm and clear during the peace-making; a warm teacher voice for Madam Salamatu
narrationPlan.pace: Quick at the start, then calm, steady, and warm (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Two lively tunes that merge into one calm tune (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Group work and shared art supplies are everyday parts of Ghanaian classrooms; learning calm conflict resolution helps every child feel heard without one child always giving way.
The six peace-making steps work in English and in every local Ghanaian language.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Confirm that neither child is forced to surrender their idea unfairly and that both contributions are valued.
Confirm that the “I feel … when …” phrasing sounds natural for Primary 1–3 learners.

teacherGuide.overview: A social-emotional classroom story teaching six practical steps for resolving everyday peer disagreements fairly: stop, breathe, say how you feel, listen, think of choices, and choose together.
learningGoals: Name the six steps for settling a disagreement calmly.
Practise using a calm “I feel … when …” sentence.
Work with a partner to combine two ideas fairly.
beforeReading: Ask: have you and a friend ever wanted to play two different games at break time? What happened?
whileReading: Practise taking one slow breath and counting silently to five together on page 2.
afterReading: Role-play a calm disagreement over sharing crayons or choosing a game using the six steps.
Create a shared pair drawing where each partner chooses one colour and explains why.
discussion: Why did shouting stop Zaara and Akrofi from hearing each other’s good reasons?
How did using both colours make their plant picture even better scientifically?
reflection: Which step—stopping to breathe or listening first—will help you most this week?

support: Display six simple gesture cues (hand up to stop, deep breath, hand on heart, hand by ear, thinking finger, handshake).
stretch: Write a four-line dialogue showing two friends solving a disagreement on the football pitch.

culturalNotes: Group work and shared art supplies are everyday parts of Ghanaian classrooms; learning calm conflict resolution helps every child feel heard without one child always giving way.
The six peace-making steps work in English and in every local Ghanaian language.
localiseThis: Practise polite peace-making phrases in learners’ home languages alongside English.
Remind learners to ask a teacher or trusted adult immediately if anyone is being hurt or bullied.
